summary: Lists requirements for performing traffic engineering over MPLS networks. It identifies the capabilities needed to use network resources efficiently and make operations reliable, guiding later protocol work. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2702 describes capabilities for steering MPLS traffic over paths that meet bandwidth and policy requirements. It sets out requirements for traffic trunks, network resources, and path selection rather than specifying a protocol.

questions: what is traffic engineering over mpls
subtitle: The capabilities MPLS needs to route traffic trunks around overloaded links.

tldr.problem: Interior routing protocols usually select shortest paths without considering bandwidth or traffic needs. This can overload some links while other feasible paths remain underused.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes traffic-trunk and resource attributes, plus constraint-based routing that selects paths satisfying the trunk's needs and network policies.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2702 presents requirements and capabilities for MPLS traffic engineering; it does not define a protocol. It is an Informational memo with no listed later update or replacement.

sections.title: The Traffic Engineering Problem
sections.content:
Traffic engineering measures, models, and controls network traffic to meet performance goals and use resources efficiently. Congestion can result from insufficient capacity, or from traffic being mapped inefficiently onto available links. Traffic engineering addresses the second problem through policies such as load balancing.

Interior gateway protocols usually select shortest paths using topology metrics. They do not account for bandwidth availability or traffic characteristics, so several streams can converge on the same links even when alternatives have capacity.
sections.plainLanguage: Shortest-path routing can send too much traffic onto the same links. Traffic engineering can select other feasible paths to use network capacity more efficiently.

sections.title: Traffic Trunks and the MPLS Graph
sections.content:
A traffic trunk is an aggregation of flows of the same class placed inside a Label Switched Path (LSP). The trunk is a routable object distinct from its LSP, so the network can move the trunk to another path. A trunk is unidirectional.

The induced MPLS graph represents LSPs as logical links between label-switching routers. Traffic engineering maps this logical graph onto the physical network. This memo focuses on mapping traffic trunks onto the physical topology, not on mapping packets to forwarding classes or those classes to trunks.
sections.plainLanguage: A traffic trunk groups flows that should be treated alike and carries them over an LSP. The network can move that group to a different LSP without changing the traffic it contains.

sections.title: Attributes That Guide a Trunk
sections.content:
Traffic-trunk attributes describe traffic parameters, path selection, adaptivity, load distribution, priority, preemption, resilience, and policing. Administrators should be able to modify these attributes. An explicit path can be mandatory, in which case setup fails if that path is infeasible, or non-mandatory, allowing an alternate feasible path.

Preemption attributes determine whether a trunk can displace another when resources are constrained. A trunk can preempt another only when it has higher priority, both need the same insufficient resource, the first is preemptor-enabled, and the second is preemptable. Resource attributes such as maximum allocation and resource classes constrain which trunks may use a link.
sections.plainLanguage: Each traffic trunk can have rules for its path, priority, recovery, and treatment when it exceeds its traffic contract. Resource rules further limit which paths the trunk may use.

sections.title: Constraint-Based Routing
sections.content:
Constraint-based routing uses trunk attributes, resource attributes, and topology information to compute explicit LSP routes that meet the trunk's requirements. It can reduce manual path configuration, while still allowing operators to specify routes for detailed tuning.

The general problem can be intractable for realistic constraints. A simple heuristic removes resources that violate the trunk's requirements, then runs a shortest-path algorithm on the remaining graph. It can find a feasible path for one trunk when one exists, but routing multiple trunks this way may fail to find a feasible mapping even when one exists.
sections.plainLanguage: The router first removes paths that violate the traffic or resource rules. It then selects a shortest path from those that remain.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says it introduces no security issues beyond those inherent in MPLS. It emphasizes that authorized entities must securely change administratively configurable parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: Only authorized people or systems should change the network's traffic-engineering settings. The memo identifies no additional security issues beyond MPLS itself.
